name: Sazerac
description: Rye (or cognac), sugar, Peychaud’s, and an absinthe-rinsed glass—New Orleans in a rocks glass.
history: A New Orleans classic with 19th-century roots. Modern home versions usually use rye; the absinthe rinse is aromatic, not a full measure.
whyItWorks: Peychaud’s anise-cherry bitters and absinthe perfume distinguish it from an Old Fashioned. The rinse should whisper, not shout.
glassware: Rocks glass (no ice in the serve)
ice: Stirred with ice; served without ice

ingredients.label: Sugar or ¼ oz simple syrup
Absinthe or Herbsaint rinse
ingredients.notes: If absinthe is out, rinse with a tiny mist of anise liqueur if available, or skip and note the aroma will be milder.

steps: Chill a rocks glass. Rinse with absinthe, discard the excess, and set aside.
In a mixing glass, combine rye, sugar (or syrup), and Peychaud’s with ice.
Stir until cold and properly diluted.
Strain into the rinsed glass (no ice).
Express a lemon peel over the drink; discard or leave per preference.
techniqueNotes: The absinthe rinse is aromatic structure—keep it light.
Without absinthe in stock, the drink is still worth making; call it a Peychaud’s rye Old Fashioned cousin.

recommendedBottles.rationale: Namesake rye—bright spice for the classic profile.
Richer rye alternative with oak depth.

substitutions.notes: Bourbon Sazerac is softer; still use Peychaud’s.
